paragraphs.heading: Air on the move
paragraphs.text: Atmospheric circulation is the movement of air on a planet-wide scale. Together with the circulation of the oceans, it is how heat gets spread across Earth's surface. The details shift from one year to the next, yet the broad layout of the flow stays fairly steady. Smaller weather systems, such as low-pressure systems in the middle latitudes, behave chaotically, so forecasts of them cannot reach past about ten days in practice or a month in theory.

paragraphs.heading: A heat engine run by sunlight
paragraphs.text: Earth's weather follows from the Sun lighting the planet and from the laws of thermodynamics. One way to picture the whole circulation is as a heat engine: the Sun supplies the energy, and the darkness of outer space is where that energy finally goes. The work this engine does moves great masses of air around. Along the way, energy soaked up by the surface near the tropics is carried toward the poles and from there out to space.

paragraphs.heading: Three cells in each hemisphere
paragraphs.text: The wind belts that wrap around the planet are organised, in each hemisphere, into three cells: the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells. Both the northern and southern halves of the planet have this set. Most of the atmosphere's motion takes place in the Hadley cell. The cells stay largely fixed because they depend on Earth's size, how fast it spins, how it is heated and how deep its atmosphere is, and none of these changes much. Even so, they move poleward in warmer periods, such as interglacial times compared with glacial ones.

paragraphs.heading: The Hadley cell loop
paragraphs.text: George Hadley described this pattern while trying to explain the trade winds. The loop starts at the equator, where the ground warms moist air, which becomes less dense and rises, leaving a zone of low pressure. Rising air from the other side of the equator pushes it toward the pole. On the way it cools, grows denser and sinks near the 30th parallel, building an area of high pressure. The air then runs back toward the equator along the surface to replace the air that rose, closing the loop.

paragraphs.heading: Trade winds and a moving equator
paragraphs.text: These flows are bent sideways by the Coriolis acceleration. High up, the air heading poleward is turned toward the east, while near the ground the air returning to the equator is turned toward the west, so it blows from the east. Those surface easterlies are the trade winds. The Hadley cell also wanders, moving north in June and July and south in December and January as the Sun heats the surface, and the belt of strongest heating is called the thermal equator. Treated as a heat engine, the Hadley system's power is estimated at 200 terawatts.

paragraphs.heading: The polar cell
paragraphs.text: The polar cell is a simple loop with strong drivers. Air near the 60th parallel is cooler and drier than equatorial air, but still warm and moist enough to rise. It climbs to the tropopause, about 8 km up at that latitude, and heads toward the pole, turning east as it goes. Over the polar regions it has lost heat by radiating it to space and is much denser than the air below; it sinks and forms a cold, dry area of high pressure. At the surface it flows back toward the 60th parallel and is turned west, giving the polar easterlies.

paragraphs.heading: Extremes and deep time
paragraphs.text: Air flowing out of the polar cell sets up ultra-long waves in the atmosphere called Rossby waves, and these steer the path of the polar jet stream. Together with the terrain and katabatic winds, the polar cell can make Antarctica bitterly cold: Vostok Station recorded −89.2 °C in 1983, the lowest temperature ever measured on Earth. Over hundreds of millions of years, tectonic uplift can reshape major parts of the circulation such as the jet stream. In the very hot climates of the Mesozoic, there may even have been a third desert belt along the equator.
